title: The Brain Doesn't Care How Clear Your Explanation Was
author: Vicky Brooks
summary: Vicky Brooks argues that the direct instruction tradition has rightly stressed clear, well-sequenced explanation but has slowly turned "clear explanations matter" into "clear explanation equals learning". Her central claim is that children arrive with mental models that feel complete to them, and the brain protects its current understanding, so it absorbs new information only when it has a reason to. Clarity is therefore the second step, and the moment before the explanation needs as much design attention as the explanation itself. She opens with a stomach-lining fact presented flat and then as a question, so readers feel the difference in their own heads. She offers three practical openers, contradiction, prediction and dilemma, each with an "instead of / try" example and a note on why it works. The content stays constant while the learner's cognitive state changes, so the explanation arrives as the answer to a question.
points: Direct instruction research is sound, but treating clear explanation as the whole of learning ignores the learner's state before instruction begins.
Because students' existing mental models feel complete, a fact lands flat until something makes the brain need it.
A contradiction, such as the pizza-slices puzzle, exposes a gap in the learner's model and creates a wish to fix it.
A prediction or a dilemma makes students commit to an answer first, so they care whether they were right when the explanation arrives.
The design question for teachers shifts from "How do I explain this clearly?" to "How do I make the learner need the explanation before it arrives?"
quotes: The acid in your stomach is strong enough to dissolve metal. So why does it not dissolve you? Did you feel that? Something shifted. Your brain leaned in. You needed the answer.
Clear explanations matter slowly became clear explanation = learning. And children have been paying the cost ever since.

Children don’t walk into our classrooms waiting for explanations. They walk in with their own explanations. Mental models about how the world works built from everything they’ve seen, heard, and experienced.

The brain actively protects its current understanding. Changing it takes real mental effort. So the brain does not absorb new information because it was explained clearly. It absorbs information when it has a reason to.
So the design question is not just: How do I explain this clearly? It’s: How do I make the learner need the explanation before it arrives?
Before you explain, students need to already be thinking, wondering, predicting, or trying to resolve something. Explanations land differently when the brain is already searching for an answer.
Why it works: predictions make the brain commit before the explanation arrives. Once you’ve committed to an answer, you care whether you were right.
The content is the same in each example. The explanation is the same. What changes is the cognitive state of the learner.
